versions.text:
The Cocoa Night

Alice and Bob lived in a small cottage at the edge of the woods. Every night, they had a special routine. Tonight was no different.

First, Bob filled the little copper pot with milk. He set it on the stove. The milk began to hum softly. Hmmm, hmmm, it went.

Next, Alice spooned in the cocoa powder. Plip, plop, went the spoon. The kitchen smelled sweet and warm, like chocolate and cinnamon.

Bob stirred slowly. Round and round the spoon went. Round and round. The milk turned soft and brown.

Then they poured the cocoa into two mugs. Each mug had a painted blue flower on the side. Alice blew gently across the top of hers. Whoosh, whoosh, went her breath, and the steam curled up like a little ribbon.

"Shall we go sit by the fire?" asked Bob.

"Yes, let's," said Alice.

They walked slowly into the front room. The fireplace crackled. Snap went a small log. Pop went a spark. The orange light danced on the wooden walls and across the soft rug.

Alice sat in the big green chair. Bob sat in the rocking chair beside her. The chair creaked, creak, creak, as he rocked gently back and forth.

They sipped their cocoa. It was warm and sweet and just the right temperature.

Then Alice looked toward the window. "Look, Bob. The sky is getting dark."

Bob turned his head. Outside, the sky was a deep, quiet blue. One small star was shining. Then another. Then another.

"One," whispered Alice.

"Two," whispered Bob.

"Three," said Alice, and she smiled. "The stars are saying goodnight to us."

They counted together, softly, slowly. Five stars. Seven stars. Eleven. The sky filled up like a blanket of tiny lights.

"I think the moon is waving hello," said Bob, pointing at a round, pale glow low over the trees.

"Hello, moon," said Alice with a yawn.

The fire crackled a little less now. Snap. Pop. Then only a soft, gentle hiss.

Bob finished his cocoa. He set his mug on the table. Clink, went the mug. Alice set hers down too. Clink.

They stood up slowly. Their feet were warm in their fuzzy socks. They walked down the hall, past the picture of the old oak tree, and into their bedroom.

Alice pulled back the quilt. It was patterned with little yellow moons. Bob pulled back his side too.

They climbed in. The mattress sighed, sooo, as it took their weight. Alice pulled the blanket up to her chin. Bob tucked it around her feet.

"Goodnight, cottage," whispered Alice.

"Goodnight, fire," whispered Bob.

From the front room came the faintest sound. A soft tick, tick, as the last embers settled. The house hummed quietly, like a lullaby no one had to sing.

Outside, the stars kept watch. The moon drifted slowly across the sky.

Alice's eyes grew heavy. Bob's breathing slowed, in and out, in and out.

Warm. Safe. Quiet.

The cottage was still. The stars were still. And Alice and Bob drifted softly off to sleep.

versions.text:
The Golden Acorn

Alice and Bob lived in a small yellow house at the edge of the woods. Every morning they looked out at the sunny meadow.

One sunny morning, Grandma came in with a sad face. "I lost my golden acorn," she said. "It was my lucky charm. Can you find it for me?"

Alice clapped her hands. "We will find it, Grandma!"

Bob unfolded an old paper map. "Here is the path," he said. "It goes across the meadow, past the big oak, and over the wooden bridge."

So they set off. Alice carried a basket. Bob carried a jar of water. The grass was tall and green, and it tickled their knees.

Soon they came to the first problem. The winding path had a gap. A little stream ran right across it.

"How do we cross?" asked Bob.

Alice looked around. She saw a long, flat log lying by the water. "Let's push it across," she said. "Then we can walk on it."

They pushed together. Push, push, push. The log slid over the stream with a soft plop. Alice went first, holding her arms out wide for balance. Bob followed, giggling. They were across!

They walked on. Bees buzzed past. A butterfly landed on Alice's sleeve and then flew away.

Then they met a small brown rabbit sitting by the path. Its ears drooped, and it looked worried.

"Hello," said Alice gently. "Why do you look so sad?"

"I dropped my shiny pebble in the bushes," said the rabbit. "I cannot reach it."

Bob pushed aside the leaves. There it was, glinting in the sun. He handed it over carefully.

The rabbit hopped with joy. "Thank you! Now you may take my shortcut through the clover." And off it went, showing them a path that was much quicker.

At last they reached the big oak tree. Its branches were wide and its shade was cool. And there, under a fat root, something gleamed.

"The golden acorn!" shouted Alice.

Bob picked it up and held it high. It shone like a tiny sun.

But the wooden bridge was next, and it creaked. The planks were old. Alice took one careful step at a time. Bob followed, counting the planks under his breath. "One, two, three, four…" They reached the other side safely.

Now the sun was going down. The sky turned orange and then pink. The grass grew quiet, and the crickets began to sing.

Alice and Bob walked slowly home along the winding path. Their feet were tired. Their basket was light. Their hearts were full.

Grandma was waiting on the porch. Her eyes sparkled when she saw the acorn. "You found it!" she whispered. She tucked it safely into her apron pocket.

Then the moon rose over the meadow, round and silver.

Alice yawned. Bob yawned too.

"Goodnight, meadow," said Alice softly.

"Goodnight, golden acorn," said Bob.

And the two of them climbed into bed, warm and safe, and drifted off to sleep.

versions.text:
Bob and the Flying Turtle

Bob had a turtle named Pickle. Pickle was small, green, and very slow.

"Pickle can fly," Bob said one sunny morning. "I just have to flap his arms hard enough."

Alice giggled. "Turtles don't have arms to flap, Bob. They have flippers!"

"Then we will flap the flippers," said Bob.

Alice looked at Pickle. Pickle looked at the grass. Nobody was sure what Pickle was thinking.

"Let's make him a cape first," said Alice. "Every flying friend needs a cape."

So they found a big sheet of paper and a box of crayons. Alice drew stars. Bob drew a lightning bolt, which was really a squiggle. They taped the cape to Pickle's shell. It crinkled every time he moved.

"Ready for takeoff!" shouted Bob.

Bob lifted Pickle up high. Then he flapped Pickle's flippers up and down, up and down, flip, flap, flip, flap.

Pickle did not fly. Pickle wiggled. His cape wiggled too. Then he slipped out of Bob's hands and went *plop* onto the grass.

"Hmm," said Bob. "He needs a bigger flap!"

Alice laughed so hard she had to sit down. "Maybe Pickle needs a rocket," she said.

So they built a rocket out of a cardboard tube, two egg cartons, and a jar lid. It wobbled. It squeaked. It looked very important.

"Blast off!" cried Bob.

They put Pickle in the rocket. Alice pushed. Bob pushed. Then they both pushed at once, *WHOOSH*, and the rocket rolled right off the table, *bump, bump, bump*, down the slope of the garden, and into a big pile of crunchy autumn leaves.

*Crunch! Swish! Splash!*

Leaves flew up everywhere. Red leaves, gold leaves, brown leaves that tickled their noses. Bob and Alice tumbled into the pile too. Then they all popped out, laughing.

Pickle poked his head out of the leaves. He had a leaf on his nose and a star on his cape. He blinked slowly.

"Pickle flew!" Bob shouted. "Sort of!"

"He flew the length of a garden," said Alice, giggling. "That counts."

They rolled in the leaves for a while, laughing until their tummies hurt. Their cheeks went pink. Pickle sat very still, enjoying his soft, crunchy nest.

Then the wind blew gently through the trees. The laughing grew quieter. The leaves rustled softly, *shhh, shhh*.

Bob yawned. "Pickle can fly tomorrow," he said sleepily.

"Maybe," said Alice, yawning too. She tucked a leaf under Pickle's shell like a little blanket.

The sun went low and golden. The garden was calm and still. Bob and Alice lay back in the leaves, and Pickle closed his eyes.

Goodnight, Bob. Goodnight, Alice. Goodnight, Pickle.

Shhh, shhh, went the leaves.

The end.
